title: Concept model A: balancing equations as bookkeeping
subject: science
phenomenonOrContext: A particle model shows hydrogen and oxygen atoms rearranging into water while every atom remains in the system.
lessonGoal: Balance chemical equations by conserving atoms and charge while changing coefficients only.
successCriteria: I count each element on both sides of an equation.
I use coefficients to scale complete formulas.
I never change a subscript to force a balance.
I verify the final equation with an atom-count table and simplest whole-number coefficients.

vocabulary.definition: a number placed before a chemical formula that multiplies the entire formula
a number inside a chemical formula that states the ratio of atoms in that substance
atoms are rearranged in a reaction but are not created or destroyed
the complete chemical formula treated as one unit when a coefficient is applied

sections.title: NOTICE — Atom counts expose the mismatch
sections.body: Start with the unbalanced representation H₂ + O₂ -> H₂O. This is a symbolic particle-accounting task; no chemicals or reaction are used.

data.readingNote: The arrow means reacts to form. Subscripts belong to the substance formula.

items.prompt: Which element's atom count is not conserved in the displayed equation?

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Count from formulas, not names
sections.body: Compare one element at a time. The two sides already contain the same hydrogen count, but the oxygen counts differ. This diagnosis identifies where balancing must begin without changing either formula.

sections.title: LEARN — Coefficients conserve identity
sections.body: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of every element and the same total charge on both sides. A coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula that follows. Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ would change water into a different substance, so subscripts are never edited to balance an equation. Coefficients describe relative numbers of particles or moles and are reduced to the smallest whole-number ratio.

items.prompt: Model task: balance H₂ + O₂ -> H₂O.

steps: Count atoms: reactants have H = 2 and O = 2; products have H = 2 and O = 1.
Place coefficient 2 before H₂O so products have H = 4 and O = 2.
Place coefficient 2 before H₂ so reactants have H = 4 and O = 2.
Verify: 2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O gives H = 4 and O = 2 on each side.
Check that formulas stayed H₂, O₂, and H₂O and that coefficients 2:1:2 are the simplest whole-number ratio.

sections.title: YOUR TURN — Nitrogen and hydrogen form ammonia
sections.body: Balance N₂ + H₂ -> NH₃. Use coefficient 1 for N₂ as the starting condition.

rows: N | count after coefficients | count after coefficients
H | count after coefficients | count after coefficients

items.prompt: After balancing with coefficient 1 for N₂, what coefficient belongs before H₂?

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Scale the whole formula
sections.body: First make the product nitrogen count match N₂ by scaling whole NH₃ formula units. Then count the resulting hydrogen atoms and choose the H₂ coefficient that supplies the same total. If you changed the 3 in NH₃, restore the formula before recounting.

sections.title: APPLY — A fresh equation
sections.body: Balance Fe + O₂ -> Fe₂O₃ using the smallest whole-number coefficients. This is a paper model only; do not attempt the reaction.

items.prompt: Write the balanced equation, provide the final Fe and O counts on each side, and explain why changing a subscript would be scientifically invalid.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Verify three constraints
sections.body: Check element-by-element equality, unchanged formulas, and the simplest whole-number coefficient ratio. If atom totals match only after editing Fe₂O₃ or O₂, the equation no longer represents the named substances and must be revised with coefficients instead.

sections.title: WHAT YOU LEARNED
sections.body: Balancing is atom and charge bookkeeping. Coefficients change relative amounts; subscripts define substance identity.

sections.title: EVIDENCE YOU USED
sections.body: You used symbolic particle models, atom-count tables, coefficient ratios, and conservation checks.

sections.title: HOW YOU DID
sections.body: Your saved coefficient and independent equation show quantitative reasoning. They remain pending assessment; copying the worked equation is not mastery evidence.

sections.title: WHAT TO PRACTICE
sections.body: Practice recounting every element after each coefficient change instead of balancing by visual guess.

items.prompt: Explain how coefficients conserve atoms while preserving chemical identity, using one formula from this lesson as evidence.

sections.title: COURSE PROGRESS
sections.body: This isolated sample does not change your course record. In a released lesson, assessed independent evidence is required before progress or mastery changes.
